title: Cain and Abel (Genesis 4:1–8)
hook: two offerings, one accepted, and a jealousy that crouches at the door

segments.voice: Yesterday: clothes for the road, God dressing the humans before they left the garden. Your line was care goes with you. Who did you send off with something? Day thirty.
screen: `CLOTHES FOR THE ROAD — CARE GOES WITH YOU.`

segments.voice: Two brothers. The older one is a farmer, the younger one a shepherd. One day, each brings a gift to God. The farmer brings some of his crops. The shepherd brings the best of his flock. And God, the story says, looks at the shepherd and his gift, and doesn't look at the farmer's. That's it. No explanation. Siblings have their own versions of this. The parent who smiled a little longer at the other one. The group chat where your news got two likes and theirs got forty. Today: the first brothers, and the thing waiting at the door.
screen: `A FARMER AND A SHEPHERD.` → `TWO GIFTS, ONE ACCEPTED.` → `NO EXPLANATION.`

segments.voice: Their names tell you something. Cain sounds like the Hebrew for acquired: his mother Eve says, I have gotten a man. Abel is hevel, which means breath, vapor, mist. It's the same word the book of Ecclesiastes uses over and over, often translated vanity. A name like a breath on a cold window, and in this story, his life is almost as short. Why was one gift accepted? The text doesn't say. But look at the wording: Abel brought the firstlings of his flock, and the fat of them, the best. Cain brought of the fruit of the ground, with no word about the best. The midrash reads the difference there: one gave the first and best, the other gave what was left. Now the part that matters most. Cain is furious, his face falls, and before anything happens, God speaks to him. Not to punish. To warn, the way you'd warn a friend. In the Jewish Publication Society's 1917 translation: "If thou doest well, shall it not be lifted up? and if thou doest not well, sin coucheth at the door; and unto thee is its desire, but thou mayest rule over it." It's the first time the word sin appears in the Torah, and it's pictured as an animal, crouching outside the door, waiting. But the last words are the hinge: thou mayest rule over it. You can master it. Then the next verse has a gap. "And Cain spoke unto Abel his brother." What did he say? The Hebrew doesn't tell us. The sentence just stops. The midrash fills it in with arguments over land, over where the Temple would stand, over a woman. The text leaves it silent. And then, in the field, Cain rises up against his brother. The first death in the Torah is a murder, between brothers, over a feeling that was warned about.
screen: `CAIN — ACQUIRED. ABEL — BREATH.` · `THE FIRST AND BEST, OR SOME.` · `SIN COUCHETH AT THE DOOR.` · `WHAT DID CAIN SAY? IT'S SILENT.` · then, large: `BUT THOU MAYEST RULE OVER IT.`

segments.voice: Two minutes, with the bell. Look for one jealous thought you've had recently. Someone's promotion, someone's marriage, someone's easy life, someone's likes. Don't argue with it and don't be ashamed of it. Just name it, quietly: that's jealousy, about that person, about that thing. Picture it crouching at the door. Then notice that you're still the one who decides whether to open it. The bell holds the time.
Hevel, Hebrew for breath or vapor, Abel's own name. The first brothers, two gifts, a warning at the door, and a silence where the words should be.
Your line: it crouches at the door. Today, when jealousy shows up, name it out loud to yourself before it gets inside. Day thirty.

howItsDone: Jews read the story of Cain and Abel in the first Torah portion each autumn, and God's warning to Cain, that sin crouches at the door but can be mastered, is often taught in Jewish discussions of free will.

fork.setup: you're Cain. your gift was passed over, you're furious, and God says sin is crouching at your door. what does God say you can do?
fork.reveal: "thou mayest rule over it." the Torah's first mention of sin comes with the claim that a person can master it.

original.note: Hebrew: Abel's name, meaning breath or vapor; Ecclesiastes' word often translated vanity.

trapdoor: what you thought: the first murder.
what it means: a jealousy warned about in advance: it crouches at the door, and you can rule over it.
what a scholar hears: 4:7 is the Torah's first use of chatat, sin, pictured as a crouching animal. 4:8 has a gap after 'Cain said to Abel'; the midrash (Genesis Rabbah 22:7) supplies the argument.

notes: Editor review 2026-10-01: the hook no longer tells the listener they "already know the feeling"; "many rabbis" replaced with the midrash the script cites (Genesis Rabbah 22:5).
Word is the outline title's head ('Cain and Abel'), kept exactly.
Genesis 4:7 and 4:8 quoted from memory of JPS 1917; confirm exact wording and punctuation.
'First time the word sin appears in the Torah' (chatat, 4:7): confirm.
The gap in 4:8 (vayomer without direct speech) is noted as silence; ancient versions supply 'let us go into the field'. A Keeper may want that mentioned.
Genesis Rabbah 22:5 and 22:7 cited from memory; confirm. The 22:7 arguments summarized as land, where the Temple would stand, and a woman (changed from the vaguer 'the future').
Why Abel's offering was preferred is debated; the script presents the first-and-best reading as 'many rabbis', not as the answer, and removed 'just some' from the description of the verse itself.
